references.text: The Lord curses the ground because of Adam, making cultivation difficult and laborious. Cain's punishment in 4:12 is an intensification of this curse—the ground will no longer yield its strength at all.
Cain was originally a farmer (עֹבֵד אֲדָמָה), which makes the curse that the ground shall not yield its strength especially personal and devastating for him.
Cain expresses despair over being driven away and becoming a restless wanderer (נָע וָנָד) on the earth, a direct result of the curse given in verse 12.
In contrast to Cain's fate as a restless wanderer, God promises to be with Jacob, watch over him wherever he goes, and bring him back to the land.
The covenantal curse involves the ground not yielding its produce, thematically mirroring Cain's punishment where the ground does not yield its strength for him.
The psalmist's curse on the wicked—that his children shall wander about and beg—reflects the theme of being a restless wanderer, like Cain's fate.
Deuteronomy 28:33 expands Cain's individual curse of losing the earth's fruit into a national judgment upon Israel.
Contrast between the chosen foreignness of the Rechabites (a lifelong sign) and Cain's forced foreignness (a curse).
Both verses illustrate the principle that rejecting God's way leads to loss of the earth's fertility or well-being.
Jeremiah 17:4 expands Cain's individual loss of land into a national judgment upon Israel.
Leviticus 26:33 shows how Cain's individual curse (scattering and destruction of the ground) can become a national judgment.
Clear contrast between God's gift of land (Joshua) and Cain's loss of the ability to cultivate the ground.
Ezekiel 33:28 expands Cain's individual ground-curse into a national devastation.
Proverbs 28:19 shows the normal law (cultivation yields bread), which Cain breaks through God's curse.
Micah 6:14 expands Cain's fate into a national judgment where one cannot enjoy the harvest or find safety.
Jeremiah 12:13 is a direct parallel to Cain's fate: the work yields no harvest (reaping thorns instead of wheat).
Jeremiah 16:13 expands Cain's individual fate as a fugitive in an unknown land into a national judgment.
Zephaniah 1:13 is a direct parallel to Cain's fate: the work brings no benefit (planting but not drinking).
Ezekiel 12:20 expands Cain's individual curse on the ground into a national devastation.
